name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Katherine Esau research on curly top virus

questiontext.text: In her early publications, Katherine Esau reported that the curly top virus spreads through a plant via which tissue?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dr. Katherine Esau's foundational research in plant anatomy focused on the structure and transport pathways of vascular tissues.

Step 2: Evaluation
In her early publications, she demonstrated that the curly top virus spreads throughout a plant via the food-conducting tissue, which is the phloem.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The curly top virus spreads through a plant via the phloem tissue.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Origin of fibrous root system in monocots

questiontext.text: In monocotyledonous plants such as wheat, the short-lived primary root is replaced by a large number of roots originating from the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Root systems in angiosperms differ between dicotyledons and monocotyledons based on the persistence of the radicle-derived primary root.

Step 2: Evaluation
In monocotyledonous plants like wheat, the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by numerous roots that originate from the base of the stem, constituting the fibrous root system.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fibrous roots in wheat originate from the base of the stem.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q03 - Characteristics of cells in meristematic region of root

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the cells present in the region of meristematic activity of a root?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A few millimetres above the protective root cap lies the region of meristematic activity, which is responsible for generating new cells by repeated mitotic division.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cells in this active division zone are characteristically very small, thin-walled, and filled with dense protoplasm, allowing them to divide repeatedly.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The cells in the region of meristematic activity are very small, thin-walled, and have dense protoplasm.

answer.text: Very small, thin-walled, and with dense protoplasm

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Function of pneumatophores in Rhizophora

questiontext.text: In Rhizophora growing in swampy areas, vertically upward-growing roots called pneumatophores help the plant to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Swampy, waterlogged soils are deficient in dissolved oxygen, necessitating specialised root adaptations for gaseous exchange.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Rhizophora, many roots emerge above the ground and grow vertically upwards; these pneumatophores help the plant obtain oxygen for respiration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pneumatophores help Rhizophora get oxygen for respiration.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Embryonic origin and distinguishing features of stem

questiontext.text: The stem is the ascending part of the plant axis that develops from the ________ of the embryo and is distinguished from a root by the presence of ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During seed germination, the embryo gives rise to the root system from the radicle and the shoot system from the plumule.

Step 2: Evaluation
The stem develops from the plumule of the embryo and bears nodes and internodes (the regions where leaves are born and the portions between two nodes, respectively), which distinguish it from a root.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The stem develops from the plumule and is distinguished by the presence of nodes and internodes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Swollen leaf base called pulvinus

questiontext.text: In some leguminous plants, the leaf base becomes swollen and is referred to as the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical leaf consists of a leaf base, petiole, and lamina, with the leaf base showing specific modifications in certain plant groups.

Step 2: Evaluation
In some leguminous plants, the leaf base becomes swollen and is called the pulvinus (whereas stipules are small lateral leaf-like structures, rachis is the common axis of a pinnately compound leaf, and scutellum is the cotyledon of monocot seeds).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The swollen leaf base in leguminous plants is called the pulvinus.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Venation in dicotyledons versus monocotyledons

questiontext.text: Leaves of dicotyledonous plants generally possess ________ venation, whereas ________ venation is characteristic of most monocotyledons.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Venation refers to the arrangement of veins and veinlets within the lamina of a leaf.

Step 2: Evaluation
When veinlets form a network, the venation is termed reticulate, which is generally seen in dicotyledonous plants. When veins run parallel to each other within a lamina, it is termed parallel venation, characteristic of most monocotyledons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Dicotyledons generally possess reticulate venation, whereas parallel venation is characteristic of most monocotyledons.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Presence of axillary bud in simple and compound leaves

questiontext.text: In a compound leaf, a bud is present in the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A compound leaf is formed when incisions of the lamina reach up to the midrib, breaking it into a number of leaflets.

Step 2: Evaluation
An axillary bud is present in the axil of the petiole in both simple and compound leaves, but it is not present in the axil of individual leaflets of a compound leaf.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In a compound leaf, a bud is present only in the axil of the petiole, but not in the axil of the leaflets.

answer.text: Axil of every leaflet, but not in the axil of the petiole
Axil of both the petiole and every leaflet
Axil of the petiole, but not in the axil of the leaflets

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Difference between racemose and cymose inflorescence

questiontext.text: Which of the following is characteristic of a cymose inflorescence?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Inflorescences are divided into racemose and cymose types based on whether the floral axis continues to grow or terminates in a flower.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a cymose inflorescence, the main axis terminates in a flower, making its growth limited, and the flowers are borne in a basipetal order. Conversely, in racemose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow and flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal succession.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A cymose inflorescence is characterised by the main axis terminating in a flower and flowers borne in basipetal order.

answer.text: Main axis continues to grow indefinitely with acropetal succession of flowers
Main axis terminates in a flower and flowers are borne in basipetal order
Main axis continues to grow indefinitely with basipetal succession of flowers
Main axis terminates in a flower and flowers are borne in acropetal order

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q10 - Definition of parthenocarpic fruit

questiontext.text: A fruit formed without fertilisation of the ovary is called a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normally, a fruit is a mature or ripened ovary developed after fertilisation.

Step 2: Evaluation
If a fruit develops without fertilisation of the ovary, it is termed a parthenocarpic fruit.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A fruit formed without fertilisation of the ovary is called a parthenocarpic fruit.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q11 - Tap root versus adventitious root food storage

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs correctly distinguishes swollen food-storing tap roots from swollen food-storing adventitious roots?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both tap roots and adventitious roots can become swollen to store reserve food material.

Step 2: Evaluation
Carrot and turnip are examples of swollen tap roots that store food, whereas sweet potato has swollen adventitious roots modified for food storage. Potato, ginger, and zaminkand are underground stems, not roots.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Carrot has a food-storing tap root, whereas sweet potato has food-storing adventitious roots.

answer.text: Tap root: Carrot; Adventitious root: Sweet potato
Tap root: Sweet potato; Adventitious root: Turnip

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q12 - Underground stems as organs of perennation

questiontext.text: Underground stems of potato, ginger, turmeric, zaminkand, and Colocasia are modified to store food and also act as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Underground stem modifications allow plants to survive periods of environmental stress when aerial shoots die back.

Step 2: Evaluation
In potato, ginger, turmeric, zaminkand, and Colocasia, underground stems store food and act as organs of perennation to tide over conditions unfavourable for growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
These underground stems act as organs of perennation to tide over unfavourable growth conditions.

answer.text: Organs of perennation to tide over conditions unfavourable for growth

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q13 - Stem tendrils versus leaf tendrils

questiontext.text: Stem tendrils that develop from axillary buds to help plants climb are found in gourds and grapevines, whereas leaf tendrils for climbing are found in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Climbing tendrils in angiosperms may be modified stems (developing from axillary buds) or modified leaves.

Step 2: Evaluation
Gourds (cucumber, pumpkins, watermelon) and grapevines possess stem tendrils, while peas possess leaf tendrils converted from leaves for climbing.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Leaf tendrils for climbing are found in peas.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q14 - Stem thorns versus leaf spines

questiontext.text: Which of the following plants has axillary buds modified into woody, straight, and pointed thorns for protection against browsing animals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants protect themselves from herbivory using sharp structures, which may be stem-derived (thorns) or leaf-derived (spines).

Step 2: Evaluation
In Citrus and Bougainvillea, axillary buds of stems get modified into woody, straight, and pointed thorns. In cacti, the defensive structures are modified leaves called spines.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Citrus has axillary buds modified into woody, straight, and pointed thorns.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q15 - Photosynthetic stems in arid regions

questiontext.text: In arid regions, plants modify their stems into chlorophyll-containing photosynthetic structures that are flattened in ________ and fleshy cylindrical in ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants in arid habitats often reduce leaf surface area to minimise water loss and shift photosynthetic function to modified green stems.

Step 2: Evaluation
Some arid-region plants modify their stems into flattened structures as in Opuntia, or fleshy cylindrical structures as in Euphorbia, both containing chlorophyll to carry out photosynthesis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Photosynthetic stems are flattened in Opuntia and fleshy cylindrical in Euphorbia.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q16 - Aquatic stem modification in Pistia and Eichhornia

questiontext.text: A lateral branch with short internodes and each node bearing a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots is characteristic of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sub-aerial stem modifications facilitate vegetative propagation and rapid spread across terrestrial or aquatic niches.

Step 2: Evaluation
In aquatic plants like Pistia and Eichhornia, a lateral branch with short internodes bears a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots at each node. In contrast, mint and jasmine have slender aerial branches that arch downwards, while banana, pineapple, and Chrysanthemum have basal underground branches growing horizontally and emerging obliquely upwards.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This lateral branch structure is characteristic of Pistia and Eichhornia.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q17 - Pinnately versus palmately compound leaves

questiontext.text: How does a pinnately compound leaf (such as neem) differ from a palmately compound leaf (such as silk cotton)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Compound leaves are divided into two types based on how the leaflets are attached to the petiole or its extension.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a pinnately compound leaf (e.g., neem), a number of leaflets are present on a common axis called the rachis, which represents the midrib of the leaf. In a palmately compound leaf (e.g., silk cotton), all leaflets are attached at a common point, at the tip of the petiole.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In a pinnately compound leaf, leaflets are borne on a common axis (rachis), whereas in a palmately compound leaf, leaflets are attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole.

answer.text: In pinnately compound leaves, leaflets are present on a common axis (rachis), whereas in palmately compound leaves, leaflets are attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole
In pinnately compound leaves, leaflets are attached at the tip of the petiole, whereas in palmately compound leaves, leaflets are arranged along a rachis
Pinnately compound leaves lack a petiole, whereas palmately compound leaves have a swollen pulvinus
Pinnately compound leaves have axillary buds in the axils of leaflets, whereas palmately compound leaves do not

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q18 - Examples of alternate, opposite, and whorled phyllotaxy

questiontext.text: Which set of plants correctly represents alternate, opposite, and whorled phyllotaxy, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phyllotaxy is the pattern of leaf arrangement at each node on the stem or branch.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. Alternate (one leaf per node): China rose, mustard, and sunflower.
2. Opposite (pair of leaves per node): Calotropis and guava.
3. Whorled (more than two leaves per node): Alstonia.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sequence representing alternate, opposite, and whorled phyllotaxy is Sunflower, Guava, Alstonia.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q19 - Expanded photosynthetic petiole in Australian acacia

questiontext.text: In Australian acacia, the leaves are small and short-lived, so photosynthesis is primarily carried out by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When leaf blades are reduced or short-lived, other leaf or stem parts may expand and become chlorophyllous to perform photosynthesis.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Australian acacia, the leaves are small and short-lived; therefore, the petioles expand, become green, and synthesise food.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Photosynthesis in Australian acacia is carried out by expanded, green petioles.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q20 - Flower symmetry in mustard, pea, and canna

questiontext.text: A flower that cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre is termed asymmetric. Which of the following plants bears asymmetric flowers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Floral symmetry is classified as actinomorphic (radial symmetry), zygomorphic (bilateral symmetry), or asymmetric (irregular).

Step 2: Evaluation
1. Mustard, datura, and chilli have actinomorphic flowers.
2. Pea, gulmohur, bean, and Cassia have zygomorphic flowers.
3. Canna has asymmetric (irregular) flowers that cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Canna bears asymmetric flowers.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q21 - Perigynous flowers and half-inferior ovary

questiontext.text: In which group of plants are the flowers perigynous with a half-inferior ovary?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Based on the position of calyx, corolla, and androecium relative to the ovary on the thalamus, flowers are hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous (half-inferior ovary), or epigynous (inferior ovary).

Step 2: Evaluation
In perigynous flowers, the gynoecium is situated in the centre and other floral parts are located on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level, making the ovary half-inferior. Examples include plum, rose, and peach. Mustard, china rose, and brinjal are hypogynous, while guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower are epigynous.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Perigynous flowers with a half-inferior ovary are found in plum, rose, and peach.

answer.text: Guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q22 - Twisted aestivation examples

questiontext.text: When one margin of a sepal or petal overlaps that of the next one and so on in a regular direction, the aestivation is called twisted. Which set of plants exhibits twisted aestivation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aestivation is the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl.

Step 2: Evaluation
Twisted aestivation occurs in china rose, lady's finger, and cotton. In contrast, Calotropis shows valvate aestivation, Cassia and gulmohur show imbricate aestivation, and pea and bean show vexillary aestivation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Twisted aestivation is exhibited by china rose, lady's finger, and cotton.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q23 - Variation in filament length in Salvia and mustard

questiontext.text: Variation in the length of filaments of stamens within a single flower is observed in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stamens in a flower may vary in their cohesion, adhesion, or filament length.

Step 2: Evaluation
There is a characteristic variation in the length of filaments within a flower in Salvia and mustard.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Variation in filament length within a flower is observed in Salvia and mustard.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q24 - Apocarpous versus syncarpous gynoecium

questiontext.text: When more than one carpel is present in a gynoecium, they are free (apocarpous) in ________ and fused (syncarpous) in ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A multicarpellary gynoecium is termed apocarpous when the carpels are free and syncarpous when the carpels are fused.

Step 2: Evaluation
Free carpels (apocarpous) are found in lotus and rose, whereas fused carpels (syncarpous) are found in mustard and tomato.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Carpels are apocarpous in lotus and rose and syncarpous in mustard and tomato.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q25 - Basal placentation characteristics and examples

questiontext.text: In which type of placentation does the placenta develop at the base of the ovary with a single ovule attached to it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Placentation describes how ovules are arranged on the placenta inside the ovary.

Step 2: Evaluation
In basal placentation, the placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it, as seen in sunflower and marigold.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A basal placenta with a single ovule defines basal placentation, found in sunflower and marigold.

answer.text: Basal placentation, as in sunflower and marigold

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q26 - Mesocarp in mango and coconut drupes

questiontext.text: Both mango and coconut fruits are drupes developing from monocarpellary superior ovaries. They differ in that the mesocarp is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In fleshy fruits, the pericarp is differentiated into an outer epicarp, middle mesocarp, and inner endocarp.

Step 2: Evaluation
In mango, the pericarp consists of an outer thin epicarp, a middle fleshy edible mesocarp, and an inner stony hard endocarp. In coconut, the mesocarp is fibrous.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The mesocarp is fleshy and edible in mango, and fibrous in coconut.

answer.text: Fibrous in mango and fleshy edible in coconut
Stony hard in both mango and coconut
Thin and membranous in mango, and stony in coconut
Fleshy edible in mango and fibrous in coconut

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q27 - Hilum and micropyle on a dicotyledonous seed

questiontext.text: On the seed coat of a dicotyledonous seed, the scar through which the developing seeds were attached to the fruit is called the ________, and the small pore located just above it is the ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A dicotyledonous seed coat has two layers (outer testa and inner tegmen) and distinct external landmarks marking its attachment and opening.

Step 2: Evaluation
The hilum is a scar on the seed coat through which the developing seeds were attached to the fruit. Just above the hilum is a small pore called the micropyle.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The scar is the hilum and the small pore above it is the micropyle.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q28 - Structure of a monocotyledonous seed

questiontext.text: In a monocotyledonous cereal seed such as maize, the single large shield-shaped cotyledon is known as the ________, and the sheaths enclosing the plumule and radicle are called ________ and ________, respectively.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A monocotyledonous embryo is situated in a groove at one end of the bulky endosperm and possesses specialised protective structures.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. The single large, shield-shaped cotyledon is called the scutellum.
2. The plumule is enclosed in a sheath called the coleoptile.
3. The radicle is enclosed in a sheath called the coleorhiza.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The structures are scutellum, coleoptile, and coleorhiza, respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q29 - Conventions in floral formula and floral diagram

questiontext.text: In a floral formula, fusion within parts of a whorl and adhesion between different floral whorls are indicated respectively by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A floral formula uses standardised symbols to represent floral symmetry, sexuality, number of parts, cohesion (fusion within a whorl), and adhesion (attachment between whorls).

Step 2: Evaluation
In a floral formula, fusion within a whorl is indicated by enclosing the figure within a bracket, whereas adhesion between whorls is indicated by a line drawn above the symbols of the floral parts.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fusion is indicated by brackets and adhesion by a line drawn above the symbols of the floral parts.

answer.text: A line drawn above the symbols; enclosing the figure within brackets
Enclosing the figure within brackets; a line drawn above the symbols of the floral parts
A dot at the top; a line drawn below G
A plus sign between figures; enclosing the figure within brackets

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q30 - Diagnostic floral characters of Fabaceae

questiontext.text: Which combination of floral characters is characteristic of family Fabaceae?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Family Fabaceae (earlier Papilionoideae) has distinct floral traits used for taxonomic identification.

Step 2: Evaluation
Fabaceae is characterised by racemose inflorescence, zygomorphic bisexual flowers, papilionaceous corolla with vexillary aestivation, ten diadelphous stamens with dithecous anthers, a superior monocarpellary unilocular ovary, and a legume fruit with non-endospermic seeds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The characteristic combination for Fabaceae is zygomorphic flower, vexillary aestivation, diadelphous stamens, and monocarpellary superior ovary.

answer.text: Actinomorphic flower, valvate aestivation, epipetalous stamens, and bicarpellary ovary
Actinomorphic flower, perianth with six tepals, epitepalous stamens, and tricarpellary ovary
Zygomorphic flower, vexillary aestivation, diadelphous stamens, and monocarpellary superior ovary
Zygomorphic flower, twisted aestivation, monoadelphous stamens, and inferior ovary

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q31 - Economic importance of Fabaceae plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following plants belonging to family Fabaceae are used as sources of dye and fibre, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plants of family Fabaceae provide pulses, edible oils, dyes, fibres, fodder, ornamentals, and medicines.

Step 2: Evaluation
Within Fabaceae, Indigofera is a source of dye, and sunhemp is a source of fibre. (Sesbania and Trifolium provide fodder; muliathi is used as medicine; soyabean and groundnut provide edible oil.)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Indigofera and sunhemp are sources of dye and fibre, respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q32 - Gynoecium and fruit features of Solanaceae

questiontext.text: In family Solanaceae, the gynoecium is characterised by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Solanaceae (the potato family) possesses a highly distinctive gynoecium morphology.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Solanaceae, the gynoecium is bicarpellary, obliquely placed, and syncarpous, with a superior, bilocular ovary containing a swollen placenta with many ovules on axile placentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Solanaceae is characterised by a bicarpellary, obliquely placed, syncarpous, superior bilocular ovary with swollen axile placenta.

answer.text: Bicarpellary, obliquely placed, syncarpous, superior bilocular ovary with swollen axile placenta
Monocarpellary, unilocular, superior ovary with marginal placentation
Tricarpellary, syncarpous, inferior trilocular ovary with basal placentation
Bicarpellary, apocarpous, half-inferior ovary with free central placentation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q33 - Economic importance of Solanaceae plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following plants belong to family Solanaceae and are used as medicine and fumigatory, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Family Solanaceae includes major food crops, spices, medicines, fumigatories, and ornamentals.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Solanaceae, belladonna and ashwagandha are sources of medicine, while tobacco is a fumigatory. (Chilli is a spice; petunia is an ornamental; Aloe belongs to Liliaceae; muliathi belongs to Fabaceae.)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Belladonna and tobacco are the medicinal and fumigatory plants, respectively, in Solanaceae.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q34 - Diagnostic features of family Liliaceae

questiontext.text: Family Liliaceae, a characteristic representative of monocotyledonous plants, is characterised by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Liliaceae (the lily family) exhibits typical monocot vegetative and trimerous floral features.

Step 2: Evaluation
Liliaceae plants are perennial herbs with underground bulbs/corms/rhizomes, linear exstipulate leaves with parallel venation, perianth of six tepals \((3+3)\) often united into a tube with valvate aestivation, six epitepalous stamens \((3+3)\), and a tricarpellary, syncarpous, trilocular superior ovary with axile placentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Liliaceae is characterised by six tepals \((3+3)\), six epitepalous stamens, and a tricarpellary syncarpous superior ovary.

answer.text: Distinct calyx and corolla, five epipetalous stamens, and bicarpellary ovary
Reticulate venation, ten diadelphous stamens, and non-endospermous seeds
Six tepals (3+3), six epitepalous stamens, and a tricarpellary syncarpous superior ovary
Zygomorphic flowers, six free petals, and inferior trilocular ovary

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q35 - Evaluate statements on root types and modifications

questiontext.text:
Read the following statements regarding roots and identify how many are correct:

(i) In Monstera and banyan tree, roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle.
(ii) Root hairs are formed by epidermal cells in the region of elongation.
(iii) Stilt roots in maize and sugarcane arise from the lower nodes of the stem.
(iv) Sweet potato stores food in modified tap roots, whereas turnip stores food in adventitious roots.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Roots are classified by origin (radicle vs non-radicle), internal developmental zones, and specialised modifications.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
- Statement (i) is correct: Grass, Monstera, and banyan tree possess adventitious roots arising from parts other than the radicle.
- Statement (ii) is incorrect: Root hairs are formed from epidermal cells in the region of maturation, not the region of elongation.
- Statement (iii) is correct: Supporting stilt roots in maize and sugarcane emerge from the lower nodes of the stem.
- Statement (iv) is incorrect: Turnip and carrot have swollen tap roots, whereas sweet potato has swollen adventitious roots.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Exactly two statements are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q36 - Evaluate statements on stem modifications

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about stem modifications is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stems undergo diverse modifications for storage, climbing, protection, photosynthesis, and vegetative propagation.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. In banana, pineapple, and Chrysanthemum, lateral branches originate from the basal and underground portion of the main stem, grow horizontally beneath the soil, and come out obliquely upward giving rise to leafy shoots.
2. In mint and jasmine, a slender lateral branch arises from the base of the main axis and after growing aerially for some time arches downwards to touch the ground.
3. Stem tendrils in gourds and grapevines develop from axillary buds, not from leaf tips or stipules.
4. Underground stems of grass and strawberry spread to new niches and form new plants when older parts die.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement claiming that stem tendrils in gourds and grapevines develop from leaf tips rather than axillary buds is incorrect.

answer.text: Stem tendrils in gourds and grapevines develop from leaf tips rather than axillary buds
In banana, pineapple, and Chrysanthemum, basal underground lateral branches grow horizontally beneath the soil and emerge obliquely upward
In mint and jasmine, a slender lateral branch arises from the base of the main axis and arches downwards to touch the ground
Underground stems of grass and strawberry spread to new niches and form new plants when older parts die

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q37 - Evaluate statements on leaf structure and origin

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements regarding leaves and select the correct set of statements:

(i) Leaves originate from shoot apical meristems and are arranged in an acropetal order.
(ii) In monocotyledons, the leaf base expands into a sheath covering the stem partially or wholly.
(iii) Long, thin, flexible petioles allow leaf blades to flutter in wind, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to the leaf surface.
(iv) A leaf is termed simple when the incisions of its lamina reach up to the midrib.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Leaves arise exogenously at nodes from shoot apical meristems and show structural adaptations in their base, petiole, and lamina.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
- Statement (i) is correct: Leaves originate from shoot apical meristems in acropetal order.
- Statement (ii) is correct: Monocot leaf bases expand into a sheath partially or wholly covering the stem.
- Statement (iii) is correct: Flexible petioles enable fluttering, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to its surface.
- Statement (iv) is incorrect: A leaf is simple when its lamina is entire or when incisions do not touch the midrib; when incisions reach up to the midrib breaking it into leaflets, the leaf is compound.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Statements (i), (ii), and (iii) are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q38 - Flower as a modified shoot and solitary condition

questiontext.text: Which of the following accurately explains why a flower is considered a modified shoot?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Morphologically, a flower represents a reproductive shoot adapted for sexual reproduction.

Step 2: Evaluation
During flower formation, the shoot apical meristem changes to floral meristem, the internodes do not elongate so the axis gets condensed, and the apex produces different kinds of floral appendages laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves. When a shoot tip transforms into a flower, it is always solitary.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A flower is a modified shoot because the shoot apical meristem changes to a floral meristem, internodes do not elongate (condensing the axis), and floral appendages arise laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves.

answer.text: The root apical meristem differentiates into floral appendages with elongated internodes
The shoot apical meristem elongates its internodes rapidly to produce leaves and flowers at the same node
Axillary buds fuse with the petiole to form a solitary thalamus
The shoot apical meristem changes to a floral meristem, internodes do not elongate, and floral appendages are produced laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q39 - Epigynous nature of ray florets of sunflower

questiontext.text: Among the following pairs, select the one in which both plants possess an inferior ovary (epigynous condition):

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In epigynous flowers, the margin of the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely and getting fused with it, so all other floral parts arise above the inferior ovary.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. Guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower are epigynous (inferior ovary).
2. Mustard, china rose, and brinjal are hypogynous (superior ovary).
3. Plum, rose, and peach are perigynous (half-inferior ovary).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both cucumber and ray florets of sunflower possess an inferior ovary.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q40 - Distinguishing parietal placentation with false septum from axile

questiontext.text: An ovary is initially one-chambered with ovules developing on the inner peripheral wall, but it becomes two-chambered due to the formation of a false septum. This condition is seen in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In parietal placentation, ovules develop on the inner wall or peripheral part of a unilocular ovary; in certain families, a false septum divides the cavity into two chambers.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mustard and Argemone exhibit parietal placentation where the one-chambered ovary becomes two-chambered due to the formation of a false septum. By contrast, tomato and china rose have true multilocular ovaries with axile placentation, and Dianthus has a unilocular ovary with free central placentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Parietal placentation with a false septum is seen in mustard and Argemone.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q41 - Endospermic vs non-endospermic seed exceptions and aleurone layer

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following statements regarding seeds:

(i) Castor is a dicotyledonous seed that is endospermic.
(ii) Orchids are monocotyledonous plants with non-endospermic seeds.
(iii) In maize, the outer covering of the endosperm separates the embryo by a proteinous aleurone layer.
(iv) Bean, gram, and pea have endospermic mature seeds.

Which of these statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Seeds are classified as endospermic or non-endospermous depending on whether endosperm persists in the mature seed.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
- Statement (i) is correct: Although most dicot seeds (bean, gram, pea) are non-endospermous, castor is an endospermic dicot seed.
- Statement (ii) is correct: Although monocot seeds are generally endospermic, orchids are an exception with non-endospermic seeds.
- Statement (iii) is correct: In cereals like maize, the outer covering of the bulky endosperm separates the embryo by a proteinous aleurone layer.
- Statement (iv) is incorrect: Bean, gram, and pea lack endosperm in mature seeds and are therefore non-endospermous.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Statements (i), (ii), and (iii) are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q42 - Construct floral formula from floral description

questiontext.text: What is the correct floral formula for an actinomorphic, bisexual, hypogynous flower with five united sepals, five free petals, five free stamens, and two united carpels with a superior ovary?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each floral feature translates into a standard floral formula symbol, with brackets indicating fusion within a whorl and a line below G indicating a superior ovary.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Translation
1. Actinomorphic \(\rightarrow \oplus\)
2. Bisexual \(\rightarrow \text{⚥}\)
3. Five united sepals (gamosepalous) \(\rightarrow \text{K}_{(5)}\)
4. Five free petals (polypetalous) \(\rightarrow \text{C}_5\)
5. Five free stamens \(\rightarrow \text{A}_5\) (no adhesion arc to \(\text{C}_5\))
6. Two united carpels with superior ovary (hypogynous) \(\rightarrow \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\)

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Combining these symbols gives \(\oplus \, \text{⚥} \, \text{K}_{(5)} \, \text{C}_5 \, \text{A}_5 \, \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q43 - Comparative analysis of Fabaceae, Solanaceae, and Liliaceae

questiontext.text: Which feature is shared in common by all three families: Fabaceae, Solanaceae, and Liliaceae?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Comparing floral and seed characters across Fabaceae, Solanaceae, and Liliaceae reveals both diagnostic differences and shared angiosperm traits.

Step 2: Evaluation
- Symmetry: Fabaceae is zygomorphic, whereas Solanaceae and Liliaceae are actinomorphic.
- Endosperm: Fabaceae has non-endospermic seeds, whereas Solanaceae and Liliaceae have endospermous seeds.
- Ovary position & sexuality: All three families possess bisexual flowers with a superior ovary (\(\underline{\text{G}}_1\) in Fabaceae, \(\underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\) in Solanaceae, and \(\underline{\text{G}}_{(3)}\) in Liliaceae).
- Placentation: Fabaceae has marginal placentation, whereas Solanaceae and Liliaceae have axile placentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All three families share bisexual flowers with a superior ovary.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q44 - Medicinal and economic plants across families

questiontext.text: Which of the following combinations of plant, family, and economic use is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each major angiosperm family has characteristic species of medicinal, ornamental, food, or industrial importance.

Step 2: Evaluation
1. Muliathi belongs to Fabaceae and is used as a medicine.
2. Ashwagandha belongs to Solanaceae and is used as a medicine.
3. Aloe belongs to Liliaceae and is a source of medicine.
4. Colchicum autumnale (source of colchicine) belongs to Liliaceae, not Solanaceae.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pairing of Colchicum autumnale with Solanaceae is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q45 - Sterile stamen and stamen cohesion/adhesion

questiontext.text:
Consider the following statements about androecium:

(i) A sterile stamen is called a staminode.
(ii) Stamens attached to petals are epipetalous, as in brinjal.
(iii) Stamens united into two bundles are diadelphous, as in pea.
(iv) Stamens attached to the perianth are epiphyllous, as in citrus.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Androecium terminology describes stamen fertility, adhesion to petals or perianth, and cohesion into one, two, or more bundles.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Statement
- Statement (i) is correct: A sterile stamen is termed a staminode.
- Statement (ii) is correct: Epipetalous stamens are attached to petals, as in brinjal.
- Statement (iii) is correct: Diadelphous stamens are united into two bundles, as in pea.
- Statement (iv) is incorrect: Epiphyllous stamens (attached to perianth) are found in lily, whereas citrus has polyadelphous stamens (united into more than two bundles).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Statements (i), (ii), and (iii) are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q46 - Developmental origin of drupes in mango and coconut

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the drupe fruits of mango and coconut?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A drupe is a fleshy fruit with a differentiated pericarp (outer epicarp, middle mesocarp, inner stony endocarp).

Step 2: Evaluation
Both mango and coconut are drupes that develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded. They do not develop from multicarpellary inferior ovaries, nor are they multi-seeded or formed without fertilisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both mango and coconut drupes develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded.

answer.text: Both develop from multicarpellary inferior ovaries and are many-seeded
Both are parthenocarpic fruits lacking a differentiated pericarp
Both possess a fleshy edible mesocarp and a thin papery endocarp
Both develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q47 - Floral diagram conventions and whorl order

questiontext.text: In a standard floral diagram, how are the position of the mother axis and the sequence of floral whorls from outside to inside represented?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A floral diagram summarises the number, arrangement, and mutual relationships of floral parts relative to the mother axis.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a floral diagram, the position of the mother axis with respect to the flower is represented by a dot on the top of the diagram. The four whorls are drawn in concentric circles in successive order from outside to inside: calyx (outermost), corolla, androecium, and gynoecium (centre).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The mother axis is shown as a dot on the top, and the whorls from outside to inside are calyx, corolla, androecium, and gynoecium.

answer.text: Mother axis as a dot on the top; whorls from outside to inside as calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium
Mother axis as a dot at the bottom; whorls from outside to inside as gynoecium, androecium, corolla, calyx
Mother axis as a dot in the centre; whorls from outside to inside as corolla, calyx, androecium, gynoecium
Mother axis as a dot on the top; whorls from outside to inside as gynoecium, androecium, corolla, calyx

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q48 - Synthesizing vegetative and floral clues to identify plant family

questiontext.text: A flowering plant exhibits roots with root nodules, alternate leaves with a pulvinate leaf base and reticulate venation, zygomorphic flowers with vexillary aestivation, marginal placentation, and non-endospermic seeds enclosed in a legume. Which of the following plants belongs to this family?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Combining vegetative, floral, fruit, and seed characteristics allows precise identification of an angiosperm family.

Step 2: Evaluation
Roots with root nodules, pulvinate leaf base, reticulate venation, zygomorphic flowers with vexillary aestivation, marginal placentation, and legume fruit with non-endospermic seeds are all diagnostic features of family Fabaceae. Among the listed plants, soyabean belongs to Fabaceae (whereas petunia and brinjal belong to Solanaceae, and tulip belongs to Liliaceae).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The described plant belongs to family Fabaceae, and soyabean is a member of this family.
